title: High Tight Flag
teaches: The high tight flag as we trade it: a quiet, liquid leader nearly doubles in a few weeks on a real change, pauses a few weeks a little under the high on lighter volume with tight closes, the buy is the trade through the pattern high at market, the stop sits a few cents under the day's low, the first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, with the rest on the trail, and a loss at the stop is the system working.

walkthroughs.title: SRPT, June 2015: the textbook pole and flag
steps: SRPT reported in May 2015, then had a 60% day. That topped a near-vertical run, up 129% in 14 sessions.
Then a 14-day sideways flag, 15.0% deep, on lighter volume, riding its rising averages. The top of that flag is the trigger.
June 10 it trades through that high. Buy at market, 27.50. Stop just under the day's low, 26.59.
A breakout nobody buys gets stopped the next session. This one: 3R on day 5. Sell into a push, trail the rest.

walkthroughs.title: SOFI, November 2024: a gap over the high
steps: SOFI ran 91% in 28 sessions in 2024, a report inside the run. Then a 7-day flag, only 9.9% deep.
The high is 14.44 and SOFI gaps over it, opening 1.5% past. That's inside our 4% line, so it's still a buy.
You buy the open at market, 14.65. Stop just under the day's low, 14.24. That's 2.8% of risk.
A close back under 14.44 says it's wrong. Instead, 3R on day 3.

walkthroughs.title: BIDU, February 2021: the push, then the trail
steps: BIDU, a big-cap, doubled in 36 sessions in early 2021. Then a 12-day flag, 13.2% deep, on lighter volume.
February 5 it clears the high. Buy at market, 264.95. Stop just under the low of the last two days, 255.06.
3R on day 2, and you hold. It runs to about 354 in three weeks. That's a push to sell into.
Then it unwinds as fast as it rose, under the flag low by late March. The 9 EMA trail gets you out.

questions.q: What are you looking at on this chart?
choices: A short rest after a near-double
A long box after a modest run
Pullbacks that keep shrinking
A sharp rebound off a crash low
questions.answer: A short rest after a near-double
questions.why: A short rest after a near-double. That's a high tight flag. IOVA more than doubled in about five weeks, then sat a little under its high without handing much back. When a stock rests like that after a run like that, the holders aren't selling. Volume dries up, the closes stay tight, and the gains from the pole stay put. These are rare. When I see one, it goes straight on my radar.
questions.lesson_line: A high tight flag is a near-double that rests a few weeks just under the high.

wrong.A long box after a modest run: That's a flat base. This one follows a much bigger, faster run and rests for weeks, not months.
wrong.Pullbacks that keep shrinking: That's a VCP, a string of smaller and smaller pullbacks. Here it's one short shelf just under the high.
wrong.A sharp rebound off a crash low: That's a V, a bounce that only wins back a crash. You want the run to start from a quiet stock.

questions.simple: A short rest after a near-double. The holders aren't selling, so it pauses near the high instead of falling.

reasons: the exact pole size differs by source (IBD 100% to 120%, Bulkowski 90%) and is a held decision, so the key avoids it

questions.story: The day before the breakout. This stock ran hard for a few weeks, and now it's resting just under its high.

deeper.counter: IBD describes a gain of 100% to 120% in four to eight weeks, then a pullback over three to five weeks. Bulkowski says it usually looks like a pause in the price rise, not a neat flag.

questions.q: On a high tight flag the stop goes at the flag's low.
questions.why: False. The flag low is the line that kills the idea, not the stop. The stop sits a few cents under the entry day's low or the prior day's low.
questions.lesson_line: The flag low kills the idea. The day's low is the stop.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: We buy at market as price trades above the peak of the ___.
questions.why: The pole. We buy at market as price trades through the pattern high, which is usually the top of the pole. IBD: the breakout clears the peak of the flagpole. Bulkowski: buy above the highest high in the pattern, usually the flagpole top. Our card adds: at least a cent over the high, regular hours only.
questions.lesson_line: The buy is above the top of the whole pattern, usually the pole's peak.
questions.simple: The pole, because we buy as price trades through the top of the run, the highest point of the whole pattern.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (entries are market orders, E57)
trigger choices are a held decision (D-027) but the key is the default every option keeps

questions.q: Check the volume bars under this rest. Volume is drying up next to the run.
questions.why: True. MRNA rested 7 days in April 2020, and volume in the rest ran 0.33x the pole's. That's about a third of what traded on the way up, and it's exactly what I want to see. The people who wanted out are mostly gone, and nobody's dumping shares into the rest. So when buyers come back through the high, there's not much supply in the way. It raises the grade. It's not a must, though. A clean flag without it still gets bought.
questions.lesson_line: Loud on the way up, quiet in the flag. That means the holders aren't selling.
questions.simple: True. Volume dries up because the holders aren't selling, and that raises the grade.

reasons: the gate (below the pole's average) is a card proposal, not an owner ruling

deeper.counter: IBD says volume generally dries up in the flag because big fund managers are holding the stock. Bulkowski finds flag volume that recedes does best.

questions.q: A stock nearly doubles in five weeks. Which start to that run do you most want to see?
choices: A quiet base, then a real change
A crash low, then a quick rebound
A late third leg in a huge run
A slow slide down to lower lows
questions.answer: A quiet base, then a real change
questions.why: A quiet base, then a real change. That's a sleeper waking up. It sat quiet for months, then earnings, a product or a contract gave big buyers a reason to show up. A run like that has real buyers behind it. A bounce off a crash only wins back what was lost, so it's a repair, not a new leg. And a third leg late in a huge run is where tired moves end. I want the sleeper.
questions.lesson_line: A sleeper that wakes up on real news is the start you want, not a crash bounce.

wrong.A crash low, then a quick rebound: That's a V. The run only wins back the crash, so it's a repair, not a launch.
wrong.A late third leg in a huge run: That's late. Most of the move is already made, and a tight flag late in a move breaks down.
wrong.A slow slide down to lower lows: A stock sliding to lower lows isn't quiet, it's weak. You want it sitting in a tight base first.

questions.simple: A quiet base, then a real change. A bounce off a crash only wins back what was lost.

deeper.example: SRPT, 2015. A +60% day on 2015-05-20, after the 2015-05-07 report, topped a near-vertical two-week run. Seven of the ten examples in our research had a report inside the pole.
deeper.counter: Kuhn: the stock sits in a well-contained base, then an important news event lifts it out of dormancy. Bulkowski found poles springing from flat bases work better, and says to avoid V shapes. Bonde warns a tight flag late in the move breaks down.

reasons: the context cue is a card proposal, not an owner ruling
Kuhn's page is a publisher store page with only the opening paragraphs public

questions.q: This rest isn't a neat flag with clean lines, just a pause under the high. It can still be a high tight flag.
questions.why: True. Don't wait for a textbook flag with neat parallel lines. TMDX ran 92% in 30 sessions, then sat just 5 days and 7.0% under the high. No pretty shape, just a quiet pause. What matters is that the rest holds near the high and doesn't hand back the run. That tells you the holders are sitting tight. Next to the steep run before it, a pause like that is tight, and that's the tell.
questions.lesson_line: Don't hunt for a pretty flag. Look for a pause that holds near the high.
questions.simple: True. A pause that holds near the high matters more than a neat shape, because it means holders aren't selling.

reasons: both Bulkowski quotes come from one author

deeper.counter: Bulkowski: a high and tight flag is often not a flag at all. It usually looks like a pause in the price rise, not a flag or pennant. IBD says the action looks tight next to the steep run-up before it.

questions.q: Your scan flags a new high tight flag almost every week. What's that telling you?
choices: Your reading is too loose
The market is just very strong
It's common in a bull run
The scan catches every real one
questions.why: Your reading is too loose. The real thing is rare. If you're lucky, you'll spot one or two in a bull market. So one a week means you're calling ordinary flags by the wrong name. That costs you, because you'll expect a rocket's follow-through from a plain flag. Measure the pole every time. A near-double in a few weeks is the bar, and most tight pauses never cleared it.
questions.lesson_line: One a week means you're calling ordinary flags by the wrong name.

wrong.The scan catches every real one: A scan finding one a week is catching ordinary flags. Find too many and your read is off.
wrong.The market is just very strong: A strong market helps. Even then, one or two in a bull market is a lucky year.
wrong.It's common in a bull run: It isn't, even in a bull run. One or two, if you're lucky.

questions.simple: Your reading is too loose. The real thing is rare, so one a week means you're naming plain flags wrong.

reasons: a count that can change (12 hits in 36 years comes from our own scan of today's tickers)
IBD's words are second-hand through Bonde

deeper.counter: Bonde, quoting IBD: if you're lucky, one or two in a bull market. And if you're finding too many high tight flags, something is wrong with your interpretation. It's rare but very profitable.
deeper.example: Our own scan found only 12 liquid ones in 36 years before 2020.

questions.q: A 30% run followed by a very tight flag counts as a high tight flag.
questions.why: False. Measure the pole first. A tight flag in a leader that never doubled is a bull flag, however tight. A high tight flag follows a near-double. A bull flag follows a much smaller run. The pole names the setup, not the tightness.
questions.lesson_line: The pole names the setup. Tightness alone never does.
questions.simple: False, because a 30% run never doubled, so even a very tight flag after it is a bull flag.

deeper.example: TSLA, 2023-07-14. A tight 8-day flag, 6.7% deep, on 0.78x volume. But the pole was 78% in 40 sessions, so it never doubled. A tight flag in a leader that never doubled is a bull flag, however tight. Best 1.88R, then stopped.

reasons: rests on the card's lookalike rule (single source)
the exact pole size is a held decision (D-048), but 30% fails every option

questions.q: How do we measure this flag's depth?
choices: Pattern high to flag low, on price
As a share of the pole's whole height
From the first flag close to the last
From the pole's low to the flag low
questions.answer: Pattern high to flag low, on price
questions.why: On price: the pattern's highest high down to the flag's lowest low, divided by that high. Kuhn measures against the advance, the pole's height. That gives a bigger number for the same flag. Kuhn's 10% to 20% limit is of the advance, so it is not the same yardstick.
questions.lesson_line: Depth is high to low on price. Measure it; do not eyeball it.

wrong.As a share of the pole's whole height: That is Kuhn's way, on the advance. It gives a bigger number for the same flag, so it is a different yardstick from price.
wrong.From the first flag close to the last: That is drift, not depth. Depth runs from the highest high to the lowest low.
wrong.From the pole's low to the flag low: That counts the whole run up as well. Depth is only the pullback, from the high down to the flag low.

questions.simple: We measure depth on price, from the pattern high down to the flag low, not as a share of the pole.

reasons: rests on a held decision (D-050, flag depth)

questions.story: The day before a breakout.

questions.q: What makes a rest like this one tight?
questions.story: The day before the breakout. The stock ran hard and has been resting under its high.
choices: Closes bunch up, wide wicks or not
Every day's range stays narrow
Each close makes a new high
Volume stays even every day
questions.answer: Closes bunch up, wide wicks or not
questions.why: The closes bunch up. Where a stock closes is where buyers and sellers settled for the day. So when the closes hold one tight area, the holders are staying put, even if the wicks swing around intraday. That's what tight means to me. On AMD here, judge the closes, not the wicks. A rest that closes all over the place is loose, and I pass on those.
questions.lesson_line: Judge a flag by where it closes, not by its wicks.

wrong.Every day's range stays narrow: Narrow days are nice, but not the test. A rest can swing wide intraday and still close tight.
wrong.Each close makes a new high: That's a climb, not a rest.
wrong.Volume stays even every day: Volume is its own read. Tight is about where the days close.

questions.simple: The closes bunch up. That's where buyers and sellers settled, so tight closes mean the holders stay put.

deeper.trap: Wide ranges don't mean a loose rest. IBD's JDSU flag had wild weekly ranges and still closed in a tight band.

reasons: the cue is IBD's and Bulkowski's; no number from our scanner is tested

questions.q: Before the breakout ever comes, the stock closes under the flag's low. The setup is dead.
questions.why: True. The flag low is the line that kills the idea. A close under it means the buyers who held the rest gave up, and the pole's gains are being handed back. There's no trade left to plan. Take it off your list and wait for a new setup to form. Don't mix that line up with your stop, though. Your stop sits a few cents under the low of the day you buy.
questions.lesson_line: Under the flag low, the idea is dead. Wait for a new setup.
questions.simple: True. A close under the flag's low means the holders gave up, so the idea is dead.

reasons: rests on the card only (single source, c16)

questions.q: Which flag top grades best?
choices: A top that is flat or slopes down
A top that climbs a little each day
A top full of loose, wide swings
A top that sags to the pole low
questions.answer: A top that is flat or slopes down
questions.why: A top that is flat or slopes down. Our card calls a down-sloping or flat top on the flag the A+ shape. Bulkowski: flags with a down-sloping top trendline tend to outperform. TraderLion says the same, with no statistics. Bulkowski also says to trade tight flags, not loose ones.
questions.lesson_line: Flat or sloping down is the A+ shape. A rising top is not.

wrong.A top that climbs a little each day: Our card names a flat or down-sloping top the A+ shape. A top that keeps climbing is not that shape.
wrong.A top full of loose, wide swings: Bulkowski: trade tight flags, not loose ones.
wrong.A top that sags to the pole low: That gives back the whole run. Our flag is a pause a little under the pole high.

questions.simple: A flat or down-sloping top, because our card grades it A+ and Bulkowski says down-sloping tops tend to outperform.

reasons: the flat-top half rests on the card only; Bulkowski and TraderLion speak of down-sloping tops
TraderLion's page could not be fetched live, so it only supports

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A trade still under 1R after ___ trading days is sold.
questions.why: 10 trading days. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money. It counts trading days, not calendar days. A trade at 1R or better is not caught by this rule.
questions.lesson_line: Give it two weeks to pay. Under 1R by then, it goes.
questions.simple: After 10 trading days, a trade still under 1R is sold so the money is free.

deeper.counter: TMDX took 23 sessions to reach 3R, but it was above 1R by day 10. The time stop sells only trades still under 1R, so TMDX would have been kept.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C33)

questions.q: You're filled on the breakout. The stop goes in as a real order with your broker right away, not later.
questions.why: True. The stop goes in the moment you're filled, as a real order with the broker. A stop kept in your head gets argued away, or missed when the stock drops fast and you're not watching. Then nothing protects the money. Buy, then stop, in the same minute. From there it only moves up, never down or wider.
questions.lesson_line: Filled, then the stop goes in at once. Never a stop kept in your head.
questions.simple: True. A real stop order protects you when it drops fast, and a stop in your head gets argued away.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D41, A4)

questions.q: What flag volume makes the A grade on our card?
choices: 60% of the pole's volume or less
About 80% of the pole's volume
A bit above the pole's volume
Any volume below the pole's
questions.answer: 60% of the pole's volume or less
questions.why: 60% of the pole's volume or less is the A grade on our card. Any flag volume below the pole's average passes the gate, and the lighter the better. MRNA's flag ran at about a third of the pole's, well inside the A zone. IBD: volume generally dries up. Bulkowski: it recedes for best performance.
questions.lesson_line: Quieter flag, better grade. Under the pole's volume is the floor.

wrong.About 80% of the pole's volume: That passes the gate but grades below A. The A grade is at most 60% of the pole's.
wrong.A bit above the pole's volume: That is above the pole's average, so it fails the gate.
wrong.Any volume below the pole's: That is the gate, the pass line. The A grade needs 60% of the pole's or less.

questions.simple: 60% of the pole's volume or less, because our card gives the A grade to the quietest flags.

deeper.example: CRNC, December 2020. Flag volume ran 0.95x the pole's, barely under it. That passes the gate, but it is only a B on this line.

reasons: the 60% A-grade line is a card proposal that can change
rests on one card line (c08)

questions.story: The day before a breakout. Look at the volume bars in the flag.

questions.q: You buy a high tight flag as it trades through the high. Where does your stop go?
choices: A few cents under the entry day's low
Under the 50-day, to give it room
A flat 8% below the price you paid
One average day's range under entry
questions.answer: A few cents under the entry day's low
questions.why: A few cents under the entry day's low, the low of the day, LOD. That's where today's buy has clearly failed, so it's the honest line. Not right on it, a few cents under, so a tick to the low doesn't shake you out. Stop first, then the size comes from it. A close stop lets the same risk buy more shares. I want it within about 3% of the buy, and it only moves up from there.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, a few cents under the low of the day. Then the size.

wrong.A flat 8% below the price you paid: That's IBD's 8% sell rule, not our stop. Ours comes from the chart, a few cents under the low of the day.
wrong.One average day's range under entry: The day's range is only a check on how wide a stop is. Ours sits a few cents under the low of the day.
wrong.Under the 50-day, to give it room: On a stock that just nearly doubled, the 50-day sits way below. That stop forces a tiny size or no trade.

questions.simple: A few cents under the low of the day. That's where the buy has failed, and a close stop buys more shares.

deeper.counter: The flag low is an acceptable stop too, but on this pattern it often sits far wider. Bulkowski's study of a stop a penny under the flag low averaged a 26% loss.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, F62)

questions.q: You're in, and the breakout day closes on light volume. That alone is a reason to sell before your stop.
questions.why: False. Light volume on the breakout day can lower the grade. It's not an exit. Once you're in, the stop is the exit, along with the time stop and the trail. You sized the trade from that stop, so the worst case is already planned. Selling on a quiet volume bar swaps your plan for nerves. Let the stop do its job.
questions.lesson_line: Once you're in, the stop decides. Not the volume bar.
questions.simple: False. The stop is the exit and you sized from it, so a quiet volume bar is no reason to sell.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, the stop is the exit)

questions.q: Bulkowski's measure rule adds half the pole to the flag low. How do you use that number?
choices: A reference, not a sell rule
My target, sell it all there
A level to add more shares
Where the first third comes off
questions.answer: A reference, not a sell rule
questions.why: A reference, nothing more. We don't trade to a price target. Even Bulkowski's perfect trades missed his measure about one time in five, since 82% of them met it. Sell everything there and you cap the big winners and still miss on some. We sell part into a push by judgment, and the rest rides the trail. The stock's own action tells you when to sell, not a projected number.
questions.lesson_line: We sell on judgment and the trail, never at a projected target.

wrong.A level to add more shares: It's not a buy level. The full size goes in at one price with one stop.
wrong.Where the first third comes off: The first sell is a judgment, not a projected price.
wrong.My target, sell it all there: We have no price target. You sell part into strength and trail the rest.

questions.simple: Just a reference. We sell part into a push by judgment and trail the rest, not at a set target.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, E51)

questions.q: Your high tight flag hits 3R on day 2. The rule is to sell the first third right there.
questions.why: False. There's no fixed sale at 3R. The first sell is a judgment. We very rarely sell on day 1, and most of the time we wait for day 3 at the earliest. Selling into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, or at about 5 to 10R, is often best. A stock doing 3R by day 2 is strong, and a push of a few days can carry it far past that. Sell a third by rule here and you cut the best part of the move.
questions.lesson_line: The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third. Let the push come.
questions.simple: False. The first sell is a judgment, most times day 3 or later, because a strong push can run far past 3R.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19)

questions.q: Bought at 27.50 with the stop at 26.59. Where is 3R?
questions.why: One R is the fill minus the stop, 27.50 minus 26.59. Add three of those to the fill: 27.50 plus 3 times (27.50 minus 26.59) is 30.23. 3R is a yardstick, not an automatic sale. SRPT got there on day 5.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 3R before the open. It is a yardstick, not an automatic sale.
questions.simple: Add three times the risk per share to the fill, which puts 3R at 30.23.

deeper.trap: Do not add three times the fill. Add three times the gap between the fill and the stop.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (B19)

wrong.$28.41: That adds one R, not three.
wrong.$29.32: That counts 3R up from the stop, not from the fill.
wrong.$31.14: That adds four R. Three R is three gaps, not four.

questions.story: Bought on the breakout.

questions.q: What's most likely behind a run like this?
choices: A real change in the business
A rally in the whole market

questions.why: A real change in the business: earnings, a product, a contract. A near-double in weeks needs a reason big buyers believe in, and a change in the business can keep them buying. Check the news on every pole. Seven of the ten examples in our research had a report inside the pole. If all you find is a market rally or a split, the move has nothing under it.

wrong.A rally in the whole market: A market rally doesn't explain one quiet stock nearly doubling. Look for what changed at that company.

A near-double off a low can still sit under it, so check before you buy. The only exception is indexes and levered ETFs, on a reversal extension or a parabolic long. Never a stock.

questions.q: Earnings come out tomorrow. Do you hold through the report?

So you're up 5R, and that's our line for holding through a report. A report can gap a stock right past any stop. A 5R cushion means a bad gap eats into profit you already have, not into your account. Under 5R, you sell before the number.

That's the full size, bought at one price with one stop. If it hits the stop, you lose about the 500 you planned, whatever the stock costs. Always round down, so the loss stays inside the plan.

questions.q: Do you buy the open?
questions.story: Your alert sits at the 60.00 pattern high. Good news hits overnight, and the stock opens at 63.30, 5.5% over the high.
choices: Pass, it's past the 4% line
Buy, the breakout is real
Buy half size at the open
Pass, never buy a gap
questions.why: Pass on the open. We never buy more than 4% over the pattern high, and 63.30 is 5.5% over 60.00. Chasing costs you size. Your stop stays where the chart puts it. So the farther up you buy, the wider the stop and the fewer shares you get. A gap inside 4% still gets bought at the open. Past it, one more way in is a morning flush that curls back up. I'd rather miss the open than chase it.
questions.lesson_line: Past 4% over the high, skip the open. Wait for a flush that curls back up.

wrong.Buy half size at the open: Half of a chase is still a chase.
wrong.Buy, the breakout is real: It's real, and it's too far away. The chase line is 4%.
wrong.Pass, never buy a gap: A gap inside 4% gets bought at the open. SOFI's was, 1.5% past the high.

questions.simple: Pass. It opened more than 4% over the high, and buying that far up means a wide stop and few shares.

deeper.trap: The alert fires at the pattern high, so the move feels like one you already own. The 4% line is measured from the pattern high, not from your alert or the news. A gap that stays inside it is still bought at the open: SOFI opened 1.5% past the high and was bought.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C28, no chasing)

questions.q: Do you buy the break?
questions.story: The flag is 12 sessions old and tight. Your alert fires on the break today. The next earnings report is in 2 days.
choices: No, the report is too close
No, the flag is too young
Yes, the flag is tight enough
Yes, and sell before the report
questions.answer: No, the report is too close
questions.why: No. We take no new buys in the 3 days before a report, and this one's 2 days out. A report can gap the stock right past your stop, and the stop can't protect you from that. A tight flag doesn't change the calendar. Check the date every time. The pole often comes off a report, so the next one can land right inside the flag. If it still sets up after the number, buy it then.
questions.lesson_line: Check the report date every time. Inside 3 days, wait.

wrong.Yes, and sell before the report: The rule is no new buy inside that window, not a quick trip in and out.
wrong.No, the flag is too young: Its age isn't the problem. The report, 2 days away, is.
wrong.Yes, the flag is tight enough: Tight doesn't change the calendar. The report window comes first.

questions.simple: No. A report is 2 days out, and a report can gap the stock right past your stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B22)
fixed before

questions.q: Where's your stop now?
questions.story: You bought at 52.00 with the stop at 51.00. Bad news overnight, and it opens at 50.40. The first 5-minute low is 50.25. The first 30-minute low is 50.10.
choices: The first 30-minute bar's low
Sell at the open, 50.40
The flag's low, to give it room
The first 5-minute bar's low
questions.why: The low of the first 30-minute bar, 50.10. When a gap opens through your stop, the first 30 minutes of that day decide. The open itself swings all over. Those 30 minutes show where buyers and sellers settle. Check the ceiling too. Your risk was 52.00 minus 51.00, and 50.10 is less than twice that under your buy. So you're inside 2R and you hold the new stop. Past 2R, you just get out.
questions.lesson_line: Gap through your stop, and the first 30 minutes set the new one.

wrong.The flag's low, to give it room: That widens the stop. The gap rule is the one exception, and it uses the 30-minute low.
wrong.Sell at the open, 50.40: The gap rule lets the first 30 minutes decide, with a 2R ceiling. It doesn't say sell the open.
wrong.The first 5-minute bar's low: Five minutes is too short. The rule uses the first 30 minutes.

questions.simple: The first 30-minute low is your new stop. The open swings, and those 30 minutes show where it settles.

deeper.trap: Check the ceiling first. If the first 30-minute bar's low were far lower, so the loss passed 2R, you would get out instead of holding.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B20)
fixed before

questions.q: A wicky breakout bar that closes well off its high grades lower than a strong close.
questions.why: True. A strong close on the breakout day raises the grade. A wicky bar that closes off its high is B-. It is a grade cue on our card, so where the day closes counts.
questions.lesson_line: Where the breakout day closes tells you who won the day.
questions.simple: True, because a strong close on the breakout day raises the grade, while a bar closing off its high is a B-.

deeper.example: FSLR, 2022-08-26. The breakout day gapped open at 125.50, over the 121.91 buy point, on 1.47x volume. It then closed at the low of its range, 121.75, back under the buy point. That is a weak close, the opposite of the strong close that raises the grade.

reasons: rests on the card only (single source, c31)
a house grading line, not a web fact

questions.q: Do you widen the stop, hold it, or sell?
questions.story: Four days after the breakout, the stock drifts back down to the pattern high. Your stop hasn't been touched.
choices: Hold, the stop is the exit
Widen it to the flag low
Sell now, before it fails
Add more at the pattern high
questions.answer: Hold, the stop is the exit
questions.why: Hold it. A drift back to the pattern high is normal. Two in three winners come back to the breakout price within a month. Nothing has broken. Once you're in, the stop is the exit, and it only moves up, never down or wider. You sized the trade off that stop, so widening it turns a small planned loss into a big unplanned one. Selling early swaps the plan for nerves.
questions.lesson_line: Until the stop's hit, the plan holds. The stop decides, not your nerves.

wrong.Widen it to the flag low: The stop never moves down. Widening it is exactly the mistake.
wrong.Sell now, before it fails: The stop hasn't been hit. Selling early swaps the plan for nerves.
wrong.Add more at the pattern high: Adding on a pullback isn't the plan. The full size goes on at one price with one stop.

questions.simple: Hold. The stop is the exit, and widening it turns a small planned loss into a big one.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, the stop only moves up)
+1 fixed before (variety rewrite)

questions.q: Does the time stop say sell?
questions.story: Ten trading days after the breakout, you're up 1.3R. It's grinding higher, not running.
choices: No, keep it, it's over 1R
Yes, it hasn't reached 3R
Keep it and add a little more
Move the stop to the flag low
questions.why: Keep it. The time stop sells a trade that's still under 1R after 10 trading days. You're at 1.3R, so it doesn't apply. Slow isn't wrong. The rule is there to free up money stuck in a trade that isn't doing anything, and this one is working. TMDX took 23 sessions to reach 3R, but it was above 1R by day 10. Let it grind.
questions.lesson_line: Slow isn't wrong. Under 1R after ten days is the line.

wrong.Move the stop to the flag low: The stop only moves up. The flag low is below it.
wrong.Yes, it hasn't reached 3R: The line is 1R after ten days, not 3R.
wrong.Keep it and add a little more: That's not the plan. The full size went on at one price with one stop.

questions.simple: Keep it. The time stop only sells trades still under 1R after 10 days, and you're over that.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C33, time stop)

questions.q: What do you do at the open?
questions.story: You bought at 40.00 with the stop at 39.00, so 3R is 43.00. The next morning it gaps up and opens at 43.60.
choices: No rule forces a sale, your call
Sell a third at the open, by rule
Sell the whole thing at the open
Wait for a dip back to 43.00
questions.answer: No rule forces a sale, your call
questions.why: Your call. A gap past 3R isn't an automatic sell. Selling part into a big gap is a choice you can make, never a rule. But look at the calendar. You only bought yesterday. We very rarely sell that early, and most of the time we wait for day 3 at the earliest. A stock that gaps up on strength right after you buy can keep running. Selling into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, or at about 5 to 10R, is often best.
questions.lesson_line: A gap past 3R forces no sale. The first sell is your judgment.

wrong.Wait for a dip back to 43.00: No rule says wait for a dip either. Judge the push itself.
wrong.Sell the whole thing at the open: That dumps the whole position the morning after you bought, right as a strong move gets going.
wrong.Sell a third at the open, by rule: 3R isn't a fixed sale point. The first sell is a judgment.

questions.simple: No rule forces a sale. The first sell is a judgment, most times day 3 or later, and a strong gap can keep running.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (F63, trim at the open)
+1 fixed before (variety rewrite)

Leave it under the entry day
Down to the flag low for room
Up to the 3R price you sold at

questions.lesson_line: First trim, then breakeven. The rest of the trade is free.

wrong.Down to the flag low for room: A stop never moves down or wider.
wrong.Up to the 3R price you sold at: The default at the first trim is breakeven, not the trim price.

questions.q: You like the setup. The stock trades 3,000,000 shares a day. What's the most you'd own?
choices: 30,000 shares, 1% of a day
300,000 shares, 10% of a day
As many as the risk size allows
No limit if the stop is tight

questions.lesson_line: One percent of the daily volume is the ceiling, however tight the stop.

wrong.As many as the risk size allows: The risk size is one limit. 1% of the daily volume is another, and you take the smaller.
wrong.No limit if the stop is tight: A tight stop doesn't help if your own selling moves the price.

questions.simple: 30,000 shares, 1% of the daily volume, so you can sell at your stop without pushing the price down.

questions.story: This stock doubled in six weeks and now flags tight. It trades at 8.40, about $35 million a day.

Take it, the dollar volume is fine
Take it at half size
Pass, the double came too fast

questions.q: Do you buy it?
questions.story: A clean flag sets up after a double, the kind you'd grade A+, your top grade. The app's market filter has read Red for two weeks. Most leaders are breaking down.

Buy a starter, add on strength

questions.why: False. The two are swapped. A VCP strings two to six contractions over 15 sessions or more after a 30% advance. A high tight flag is one shelf a little under the high of a near-double pole.

questions.q: Do you take it?
questions.story: The stock was already up several hundred percent in the six months before this run began. Now it doubles again and pauses tight.
choices: Pass, it's too late in the move
Pass, tight flags are traps
Take it, it's a fresh first base
Take it, momentum makes it sure
questions.answer: Pass, it's too late in the move
questions.why: Pass. It's late. The stock had already run several hundred percent before this pole even started. Most of the move is made, so there's little left to gain and a lot to give back if it turns. A tight flag after a run like that is where tired moves end. Tight doesn't fix late. I want the first or second big leg, not the third.
questions.lesson_line: Early legs pay. A flag after a giant run is where tired moves end.

wrong.Take it, it's a fresh first base: Up several hundred percent isn't fresh. Ask whether it's the first base.
wrong.Take it, momentum makes it sure: Nothing's sure. Momentum this late is the risk.

A trade above the highest high
A buy at the next day's open
A close above the pole top

questions.why: Buying a trendline break inside the flag. Bulkowski found too many of these fail to move higher, even after the line breaks. It feels smart because it's early, but it buys before the stock has proven anything. His fix is ours: buy as price trades through the highest high of the pattern. We buy at market right as it goes through, during the day. We don't wait for the close.

wrong.A trade above the highest high: That's the entry he recommends, and ours.
wrong.A buy at the next day's open: That's a timing choice. His warning is about the line inside the flag.
wrong.A close above the pole top: He uses a close above the top to confirm the pattern, not to reject it.

deeper.trap: Some chart vendors teach an early entry: buy the break of the down-sloping line inside the flag. It feels smarter because it's earlier. Bulkowski found too many of these fail to move higher even after the line breaks. So the trigger is the pattern high, not the line.

The volume test: above the pole's
questions.answer: The flag length: not 5 to 30 sessions
questions.why: The flag length. Our card allows a rest of 5 to 30 sessions, and this one ran 32. Past 30 sessions it is a different base, graded as that base. It passes the other tests. A near-miss that ran well is still not this setup.
questions.lesson_line: A flag rests a few weeks. A much longer rest is a different base, graded as that base.

wrong.The flag depth: deeper than 25%: The rest is 23.1% deep, inside our 25% limit. Only one test fails.
wrong.The closes test: wider than 10%: The closes were tight, so the 10% test passes. Only one test fails.
wrong.The volume test: above the pole's: The volume test passes. Only one test fails, and it is the length.

questions.simple: It fails the flag length, because past 30 sessions the rest has become a different base.

deeper.trap: Count the rest in sessions. Our card allows 5 to 30. IBD gives three to five weeks and Kuhn three to six, so 32 sessions is past even Kuhn's longest flag.

reasons: rests on a held decision (D-049, flag length)
fixed before

questions.q: Buy the pause, or not?
questions.story: The pole's last three days were all up days, each a gap up on rising volume and a wider range. The last one, the climax day, closed below its open. Now it pauses.
choices: Not; it reads as a parabolic top
Not; a gap means the move is over
Buy it; the pause is very tight
Buy over the climax day's high
questions.answer: Not; it reads as a parabolic top
questions.why: Not. The last leg of the pole was a burst: gap ups, rising volume and wider ranges. The climax day closed below its open. Our card calls that a possible parabolic top, not a flag. A pause afterward does not cancel the reversal.
questions.lesson_line: Read the last leg of the pole. A burst that reverses is a top, not a flag.

wrong.Buy over the climax day's high: The trigger is fine on a flag. This is not a flag.
wrong.Not; a gap means the move is over: Gaps alone do not end a move. SOFI gapped over its pattern high and ran to 6.2R. The warning is the climax day closing below its open.
wrong.Buy it; the pause is very tight: Tight does not cancel the reversal. The card calls it a possible top.

questions.simple: Not, because the pole ended in a burst and the climax day closed below its open, which marks a possible top.

deeper.trap: The trap is the tidy pause. A tight pause looks like a flag, so the eye skips the last leg. The card reads that leg first. A burst of gap ups, then a climax day that closed below its open, is a possible top. It is not a flag.

reasons: rests on the card's parabolic-top test only (c18, c42)
a proposed test, not an owner ruling

questions.q: Which card fits?
questions.story: The stock rose 35% in six weeks. Then it tightened for four weeks with higher lows, riding its rising short averages.
choices: The Qullamaggie breakout
High tight flag setup
A V off a crash low
A flat base or a cup
questions.why: The Qullamaggie breakout. It needs only a 30% move in the past 1 to 3 months and rests 2 weeks to 2 months. A high tight flag needs the double in 8 weeks or less. This stock rose 35% in six weeks, so it fits his breakout, not the near-double. His stock surfs the rising 10- and 20-day through the rest, and we draw the 9 and 20 EMA.
questions.lesson_line: The pole decides which card you are on.

wrong.High tight flag setup: 35% is nowhere near a double. The flag needs the near-double first.
wrong.A V off a crash low: Nothing here fell. It rose and tightened.
wrong.A flat base or a cup: A base that lost the fast averages is a flat base or a cup. This one rides its rising short averages.

questions.simple: The Qullamaggie breakout, because it needs only a 30% move, while the high tight flag needs a double.

deeper.trap: The trap is the shared look. Both end in a tight pause near the high, so the chart alone does not name the card. Measure the pole. His breakout needs a 30% move in the past 1 to 3 months. The high tight flag needs the double in 8 weeks or less.

reasons: the card's summary of his breakout; his page gives 30% to 100%+ in 1 to 3 months
the near-double size is a held decision (D-048), but 35% fails every option

questions.q: Do you take it?
questions.story: The stock fell 55% in six weeks. Then it doubled off the low in five weeks, and now it pauses near the high.
choices: Pass, it's a V off a crash
Take it, the pole doubled
Take it, the flag is tight
Pass, the run was too fast
questions.answer: Pass, it's a V off a crash
questions.why: Pass. That double is a rebound off a crash. A stock that drops 55% has to more than double just to get back where it was. So the run only repairs the damage. It's not a fresh launch from a quiet base. And everyone who bought on the way down is sitting above you, waiting to get out even. I want the sleeper that wakes up, not the wreck that bounces.
questions.lesson_line: A double off a crash is a repair, not a launch.

wrong.Take it, the pole doubled: The double's real, but it starts from a crash. That's a V.
wrong.Take it, the flag is tight: A tight flag doesn't fix where the pole began.
wrong.Pass, the run was too fast: Fast is part of this pattern. The problem's the crash before it.

questions.simple: Pass. A double off a crash only repairs the fall, so it's not a launch from a quiet base.

deeper.trap: The trap is the double. A pole that doubles looks like the pattern, but a double off a crash low only repairs the damage. Check what came before it: Bulkowski says to avoid V shapes, where price drops hard into the pole.

reasons: Bulkowski independently says to avoid V shapes; the card's 30% fall line is no longer tested

questions.q: What do you do?
questions.story: You bought the breakout at 52.01 with the stop at 49.95. The run before it was 291% in 34 sessions, then six days of rest. Breakout volume was a tenth of normal. Next morning it hits your stop.
choices: Sell at the stop, as planned
Hold, the pole was huge
Widen the stop to the flag low
Buy more, it's cheaper here
questions.answer: Sell at the stop, as planned
questions.why: Sell at the stop. That's the plan, and the stop is the exit. You sized the trade off 49.95, so this loss is the one you already agreed to. SRRK in December 2020 had the biggest pole in our research. But the breakout day traded about a tenth of its average volume, and nobody showed up. Stopped the next session. A huge pole is a reason to buy, never a reason to hold past the stop.
questions.lesson_line: The stop is an appointment, not a debate. Even after a perfect-looking pole.

wrong.Widen the stop to the flag low: The stop only moves up. Widening it would be the mistake.
wrong.Hold, the pole was huge: The pole doesn't move the stop. The stop is the exit.
wrong.Buy more, it's cheaper here: That's adding to a loser, and this one is going through its stop.

questions.simple: Sell at the stop. You sized the trade from it, and a huge pole doesn't change the plan.

deeper.trap: A perfect-looking pole. 291% in 34 sessions was the biggest pole in our research, and the flag was 6 days and 15.5% deep. None of that moves the stop. A pole is a reason to buy, never a reason to hold past the stop. The breakout day traded 0.10x its 50-day average, and quiet volume only lowers the grade.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, the stop is the exit)
+2 held decision D-006 (breakout volume as a gate)

questions.q: Next morning it takes your stop. Was buying the gap a mistake?
questions.story: A high tight flag that checks every box gaps open at 125.50, over the 121.91 buy point, on 1.47x volume. You're filled, stop 120.92. It closes at 121.75, near the low of its day.
choices: No, a planned loss at the stop
Yes, skip gaps next time
No, but widen the stop next time
Yes, volume was too quiet
questions.answer: No, a planned loss at the stop
questions.why: No. A gap over the buy point that stays inside 4% gets bought at the open, and 125.50 was inside that line. The stop is the exit, and you sized the trade so a stop-out costs only what you planned. FSLR in August 2022 traded down to 118.13 the next session and took the stop. Closing near the low of the day was a weak sign. The buy was still right. A loss at the stop is the system working.
questions.lesson_line: A loss at the stop is the cost of being there for the ones that work.

wrong.Yes, skip gaps next time: A gap inside 4% gets bought at the open. SOFI's did, and it ran.
wrong.No, but widen the stop next time: A wider stop means fewer shares, not a better trade.
wrong.Yes, volume was too quiet: It broke out on 1.47x volume, well above average.

questions.simple: No. A gap inside the 4% line is bought at the open, and a loss at the stop is a cost you planned.

deeper.trap: Judging the trade by its result. The gap was bought by the rule, inside the 4% line, so the loss was a planned cost. The bar did close at the low of its day, back under the buy point, a weak close. SOFI also gapped, 1.5% past the high, and reached 3R on day 3.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C28, 4% line; A4, the stop is the exit)

questions.q: Was the loss a mistake?
questions.story: You bought the breakout at 175.81 with the stop at 168.86. It runs to 2.35R, then rolls over. On day 3 it trades through your stop.
choices: No, the stop was the planned exit
No, but skip this stock next time
Yes, you should've sold at 2R
Yes, widen the stop next time
questions.answer: No, the stop was the planned exit
questions.why: No. The stop was the exit, and you sized from it, so the loss was the amount you chose to risk. MRVL in May 2026 peaked at 2.35R and gave it all back. That happens. The first sell is a judgment, and most of the time we wait for day 3 at the earliest. What you could have done is move the stop to breakeven. That's allowed anywhere from 2R to 5R, or at the first sell, and it's your call. Do it at 2R and this one's a scratch.
questions.lesson_line: A trade that hits 2R and comes back is a planned loss, or a scratch.

wrong.Yes, you should've sold at 2R: No rule sells at 2R. The first sell is a judgment.
wrong.Yes, widen the stop next time: A wider stop means fewer shares, not a better trade.
wrong.No, but skip this stock next time: A stop-out isn't a ban. A new trigger is a new trade.

questions.simple: No. The stop was the planned exit, and sizing from it kept the loss to the risk you chose.

deeper.counter: The same trade with the stop moved to breakeven at 2R would have been a scratch. That's allowed anywhere from 2R to 5R, or at the first sell. It's a choice to give back less, not proof that the buy was wrong. MRVL, May 2026: bought at 175.81, best 2.35R, stopped on day 3 at a low of 165.10.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, breakeven window)
+2 held owner question: should breakeven at 2R be the default?

questions.q: Why did this one lose?
questions.story: A 101% pole, then a 15-day flag 8.5% deep. You buy the breakout at 398.90 on 1.48x volume, stop 386.96. It reaches 1.66R, then stalls. On day 7 it trades through your stop.
choices: A valid flag simply failed
The stop was set too tight
The first trim came too late
The pole was too small
questions.why: A valid flag that simply failed. The pole more than doubled and the flag was tight. Be honest about the buy day, though. It closed back under your fill, well off the high, with a long upper wick. That's a warning, not a broken setup. MDB in June 2023 got to 1.66R, stalled, and hit the stop on day 7. Many of these fail. That's why the stop and the size do the real work. You sized from the stop, so the loss was the risk you picked.
questions.lesson_line: Not every good setup works. The stop is what makes that fine.

wrong.The pole was too small: The pole more than doubled. The setup was valid.
wrong.The stop was set too tight: A wider stop means fewer shares, not a setup that works.
wrong.The first trim came too late: It never pushed. It topped at 1.66R, so no sale came late.

questions.simple: A valid flag that simply failed. Sizing from the stop kept the loss to the risk you chose.

deeper.trap: Treating a failure as an error. Reaching 1.66R and then stalling is a normal path for a flag that fails. IBD warns that many fail, so the stop and the size do the real work. Changing the rules after one stop-out would not have saved this trade. MDB, June 2023: best 1.66R, stopped on day 7.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A4; the stop sets the size)

questions.q: What does that heavy volume in the rest mean for your plan?
questions.story: The day before the breakout. A 123% pole, then a 16-day flag 17.2% deep. Volume in the flag runs 1.27x the pole's average. A grade is your judgment of how clean a setup is, and it sets the size.
choices: A warning that can lower the grade
A sell signal, the setup is void
A buy signal, volume means interest
Nothing, volume doesn't count here
questions.answer: A warning that can lower the grade
questions.why: It's a warning, and it can lower the grade. In a rest I want volume drying up. Here the flag traded 1.27x the pole's average, so more shares are changing hands in the rest than on the way up. Someone's selling into it. That doesn't void the setup, because volume only moves the grade. A lower grade means a smaller size. PDD in December 2020 had this look and never got going, best 0.0R, stopped.
questions.lesson_line: Heavy volume in the rest is a warning and a lower grade, not a ban.

wrong.A sell signal, the setup is void: Heavy volume in the rest doesn't void it. It's a warning and a lower grade.
wrong.A buy signal, volume means interest: In a rest we want volume drying up. Heavy volume there is selling, not interest.
wrong.Nothing, volume doesn't count here: Volume counts. It raises or lowers the grade. It's just not a must.

questions.simple: A warning that lowers the grade. Volume should dry up in a rest, but this doesn't void the setup.

deeper.trap: The trap is the huge pole. A 123% pole feels like proof, but it only shows the stock can run. The flag shows who is selling. PDD's flag volume ran 1.27x the pole's average, and the trade reached 0.0R at best before it was stopped.

reasons: rests on his rulings that volume only raises the grade (D-006) and that a heavy-volume day is a warning, never an invalidation

questions.q: High tight flag, or something else?
questions.story: A 99% pole, then a 24-day flag 12.7% deep on light volume. Five closes in the flag sit under the 21-day EMA.
choices: A flat base or a cup
A high tight flag
A bull flag
questions.answer: A flat base or a cup
questions.why: A flat base or a cup. Five flag closes sat under the 21-day EMA. A base that lost the fast averages is a flat base or a cup, not a high tight flag.
questions.lesson_line: A real flag rides its fast averages. Lose them and it is a different base.

wrong.A high tight flag: The flag should hold the 21-day EMA. Five closes under it fail that line.
wrong.A bull flag: Measure the pole: a bull flag follows a 20% to 30% run, not a near-double.

questions.q: Which grades higher on volume?
questions.story: Two flags after a double. Flag A trades 45% of the pole's average volume. Flag B trades 95% of it.
choices: Flag A, the quieter flag
Flag B, the busier flag
The same; both pass the gate
Neither; both fail the gate
questions.why: Flag A. Both pass the gate, because flag volume below the pole's average is required. Flag A trades 45% of the pole's average, so it earns the A grade, which is flag volume at most 60% of the pole's. Flag B trades 95%, a B on that line. CRNC's flag volume was 0.95x the pole's, barely under it: a B on that line.
questions.lesson_line: Both pass the gate. The quieter flag earns the higher grade.

wrong.Flag B, the busier flag: Heavier flag volume is less drying up. It passes the gate but grades lower.
wrong.The same; both pass the gate: Passing the gate is not the same grade. The card grades the lighter flag higher.
wrong.Neither; both fail the gate: Both sit below the pole's average, so both pass. The 60% line is only the A grade.

questions.simple: Flag A, because quieter flag volume earns a higher grade, and only Flag A is at 60% or less of the pole's.

deeper.trap: The trap is stopping at the gate. Both flags pass it, so it is easy to call them equal. The card grades by how quiet the flag is, and 60% or less of the pole's volume is the A. CRNC's flag ran at 0.95x the pole's and got a B on this line.

reasons: the 60% A-grade line is a card proposal that can change
rests on one card line (c08)

questions.q: Which context grades higher?
questions.story: Two stocks double in seven weeks. One runs on a news story with no earnings behind it. The other runs on a big earnings beat on heavy volume.
choices: The earnings beat
The news story
They grade the same
Neither can be traded
questions.why: The earnings beat. A real change behind the pole (earnings, a product, a contract) with heavy volume is the A+ context. A news-only story with no earnings is B-. Growth or a real catalyst is preferred, not required, and the chart comes first. Bonde: weigh the earnings and whether it is the first base.
questions.lesson_line: Ask why it doubled. Earnings beat a headline.

wrong.The news story: A news-only story with no earnings is B- context on our card.
wrong.They grade the same: The pole's cause is a grade cue. A real change grades higher.
wrong.Neither can be traded: Earnings are preferred, not required. A news-only story is graded B-, not banned.

questions.simple: The earnings beat grades higher, because a real change in the business with heavy volume beats a story with no earnings.

deeper.counter: A news-only pole is not banned. It is graded B-, and the chart still comes first. Bonde: weigh the earnings and whether it is the first base. Seven of the ten examples in our scan had a report inside the pole, so earnings are the usual cause, not the only one.

reasons: +2 held decision D-007 and proposed card grades (A+ versus B-)
+2 the grades are the card's proposal, not an owner ruling

questions.q: Do you buy the break?
questions.story: A fast pole, then a flag of eight sessions, 18% deep. At the pattern high, price sits 11% above the 9 EMA.
choices: Pass, it's too stretched
Pass, the flag is too deep
Buy, it's clearing the high
Buy with a wider stop for room
questions.why: Pass. We skip a long more than 10% over its 9 EMA, and this one's 11% over. That holds even right at the pattern high. A stock that stretched can snap back to its average fast, and that pullback comes out of your pocket. The break is real, and the 18% depth isn't the issue. The stretch is. Let the 9 EMA catch up, and buy the next tight trigger.
questions.lesson_line: A clean break can still be too stretched. Over 10% above the 9 EMA, pass.

wrong.Buy with a wider stop for room: A wider stop doesn't fix a stretched entry. It just shrinks the size.
wrong.Buy, it's clearing the high: The break is real, but the stretch says skip it.
wrong.Pass, the flag is too deep: At 18% the depth isn't what stops this buy. The stretch is.

questions.simple: Pass. It's 11% over the 9 EMA, past our 10% line, and a stretched stock snaps back harder.

deeper.counter: An 18% flag sits inside IBD's usual 10% to 20%.
deeper.trap: Two separate rules. Never buy more than 4% above the buy point. Skip a long more than 10% above its 9 EMA. A buy at the pattern high can pass the first and still fail the second.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C29)
fixed before

questions.q: What do you do with the rest?
questions.story: Two weeks after the breakout, the stock gaps up three days in a row on rising volume. You've already sold part.
choices: Sell a big part into the burst
Hold it all for the trail
Add on strength, it's working
Move the stop to the flag low
questions.answer: Sell a big part into the burst
questions.why: Sell a big part into it. A climax run on your own long is when you sell into the buyers. It's a judgment call, but these breakouts often go vertical, and vertical is the most stretched the run gets. Sell while the buyers are eager. Wait for the trail and you're selling after it turns, and these can fall back as fast as they went up. What's left stays on the trail. Don't add into a burst like this.
questions.lesson_line: When it goes vertical, sell into the buyers. Don't wait for the trail.

wrong.Hold it all for the trail: The trail sells after the burst turns, not into it.
wrong.Move the stop to the flag low: The stop only moves up, and the flag low is far below.
wrong.Add on strength, it's working: Not into a vertical burst. That's where you sell, not buy.

questions.simple: Sell a big part into the burst. Vertical is the most stretched it gets, and it can fall just as fast.

deeper.trap: Waiting for the trail. The trail is a close below the 9 EMA or the 20 EMA. That sells after the burst has turned, not into it. A climax run can fall back as fast as it rose. So you sell a big part into the burst, and it's a judgment call.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C34, a judgment call)

questions.q: What gets you out of the rest?
questions.story: You bought at 264.95 with the stop at 255.06. You sold part into the push, and the rest still rides. Later it ran to about 354 and turned down hard.
choices: A close below the trail average
A close under the flag low
A close back at your 3R price
Nothing, hold on for a double
questions.answer: A close below the trail average
questions.why: A close below your trailing average. Once you've sold some into the push, the rest rides the trail. On a fast mover like this that's the 9 EMA, on a steadier one the 20 EMA. A close under it says the push is done, so you sell what's left before a fast run hands back its gains. BIDU ran to about 354 in three weeks, then collapsed under the flag low by late March. The trail gets you out long before that.
questions.lesson_line: These rockets come back as fast as they went up. The trail is your exit.

wrong.A close under the flag low: By then most of the run is gone. BIDU fell under it by late March.
wrong.A close back at your 3R price: That's not an exit rule. What's left rides the trail.
wrong.Nothing, hold on for a double: Hoping isn't an exit. These rockets come back as fast as they went up.

questions.simple: A close below the trailing average. It says the push has stalled, so you sell before the run gives more back.

deeper.example: BIDU, February 2021. Bought at 264.95, stop 255.06. It reached 3R on day 2 and 5R after that. It ran to about 354 within three weeks, then collapsed under the flag low by late March. The trail is what gets you out of what is left.

reasons: +2 held decision D-024 (which average is the trail)

questions.q: In our scan of 54 hits, most reached 3R before the stop.
questions.why: False. 16 of 54 hits (29.6%) reached 3R before the stop, and 12 of 54 (22.2%) reached 5R, on a fixed stop with no trims. IBD: high tight flags are high-risk bases, and many fail.
questions.lesson_line: Most hits stall before 3R. The stop and the size do the real work.
questions.simple: False, because only 29.6% of the 54 hits in our scan reached 3R before the stop.

deeper.trap: A base rate is not a forecast. In our own scan of 54 hits on a fixed stop with no trims, 29.6% reached 3R and 22.2% reached 5R. Read what a statistic measured before you lean on it.

reasons: +2 rests on our own scan (d23), a Tier 3 fact
+1 the scan figures change with the data

questions.q: A reader tested these with a mechanical scan. What was Bonde's reply?
choices: Late flags fail; context decides
The scan is right; avoid them all
Trade the scan as a mechanical system
Early flags fail; late flags work
questions.why: Late flags fail; context decides. Bonde: if a tight flag appears late in the move, it will break down. He adds that you must weigh the earnings and whether it is the first base. He says it cannot be traded as a mechanical system, because the interpretation becomes critical. Our not-late test applies this: the pole must be the first or second big leg.
questions.lesson_line: The pattern is the start. The context decides whether it is ours.

wrong.The scan is right; avoid them all: Bonde did not drop the pattern. He called it rare but very profitable and said the reading becomes critical.
wrong.Trade the scan as a mechanical system: Bonde said the opposite: it cannot be traded as a mechanical system.
wrong.Early flags fail; late flags work: Backwards. Bonde: a tight flag late in the move breaks down.

questions.simple: Bonde said late flags tend to fail, so you must judge the context, since it cannot be traded as a mechanical system.

deeper.trap: The trap is trusting the scan. A scan can find 'doubled, then tight' mechanically, but it cannot see where the flag sits in the move. Bonde's two checks are the earnings and whether it is the first base. Our card turns the second into a gate: the pole is the first or second big leg.

reasons: all three quotes come from one Bonde post (single source)
the reader's scan is described only on that page

questions.q: You're up 3.5R on a high tight flag. Earnings come out later this week. Do you hold through the report?
choices: Sell it all before the report
Sell half, hold the rest
Hold it, 3.5R is enough cushion
Hold it, with the stop at breakeven
questions.answer: Sell it all before the report
questions.why: Sell it before the report. We hold through a report only when the trade's up 5R, and 3.5R is short of that. A report can gap the stock hard against you and jump right past any stop, breakeven or not. 5R is the cushion that makes a bad gap survivable. And if it still sets up after the number, you can buy it back.
questions.lesson_line: Up 5R rides through a report. Anything less, you sell first.

wrong.Hold it, with the stop at breakeven: A gap jumps the stop, breakeven or not. It doesn't lift you to 5R.
wrong.Sell half, hold the rest: Holding any part breaks the rule. Only a trade up 5R holds through.
wrong.Hold it, 3.5R is enough cushion: Being a winner isn't enough. The line is 5R.

questions.simple: Sell it. Only a trade up 5R holds through a report, because a gap can jump your stop.

deeper.trap: Judge the cushion in R, not by the chart. A third may be off and the stop at breakeven, yet the report rule still says sell. Only 5R carries a trade through.

reasons: one cited fact only
rests on the owner's rulebook (B22)

questions.q: Can you take it again?
questions.story: You got stopped out the day after a breakout. Two weeks later the stock builds a fresh tight flag and trades through its high.
choices: Yes, as a new trade, new stop
No, it already failed once
Yes, double size to make it back
No, wait a full month first
questions.answer: Yes, as a new trade, new stop
questions.why: Yes, as a new trade. A fresh trigger is new evidence. The first try didn't work, and the stop told you so cheaply. It's a new setup, so it gets its own stop under the new day's low, its own size, and every rule again. The cap is 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month on one stock. That keeps a stubborn name from bleeding you.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-out isn't a ban. A new trigger is a new trade.

wrong.No, it already failed once: One stop-out doesn't end the stock. A new trigger is a new trade.
wrong.Yes, double size to make it back: Size comes from the new stop and your risk, never from making it back.
wrong.No, wait a full month first: No rule sets a waiting period. A new trigger is a new trade.

questions.simple: Yes, if it triggers again. A new trigger is new evidence, and the new stop sets the new risk.

deeper.trap: Revenge. After a stop-out the pull is to win it back with more size or the old stop. A new trigger is a new trade. It gets its own stop under the new day's low, its size from that stop, and every rule again. The cap is 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month on one stock.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B21 and E56)

questions.q: Do you take it?
choices: Take it, the pole doubled
Take it, flag volume is rising
Pass, the run is far too small
Pass, the flag is far too deep
questions.why: Take it. SRPT ran 129% in 14 sessions, a real double in about three weeks. Then it rested 14 days, sideways, 15.0% off the high. Volume in the rest dried up to 0.66x the pole's, so the holders weren't selling. Yes, it's a long way over its moving averages. After a double, that's what a high tight flag looks like. Now look at the last candle. An inside day, closing near its high, right under the high of the flag. That's a good look the day before a buy day. Buy it as it trades through the high, stop a few cents under the low of the day.
questions.lesson_line: Count the pole first. A real double, then a quiet shelf, that's the setup.

wrong.Pass, the run is far too small: The run was well over a double, in a few weeks.
wrong.Pass, the flag is far too deep: 15.0% off the high is a normal depth for this one.
wrong.Take it, flag volume is rising: Flag volume ran 0.66x the pole's. That's drying up, not rising.

questions.simple: Take it. It more than doubled fast, then rested with volume drying up, so the holders stayed put.

questions.q: The day before it trades through a tight flag's high. Weigh the last 8 weeks. Take it as a high tight flag, or pass?

Take it; the flag is tight
Take it; it is a strong leader
Pass; flag volume is too heavy

questions.story: A leader rose 110% over 14 weeks, off a quiet base, after an earnings beat. Since then it has rested tight just under the high.
choices: The time test: too many weeks
The size test: too small
The base test: not quiet
The cause test: no change

choices: Weekly closes bunched together
Narrow daily ranges every bar
Light volume on each flag day
A gap up through the flag top

Light volume grades the flag's volume, and a gap is a trigger event. Neither is the tightness cue.

questions.q: Do you buy it?
questions.story: The chart checks every box: a double in seven weeks off a quiet base, a tight flag, and a trigger. A big new contract drove the run. But sales growth stalled last quarter.
choices: Buy it, the chart comes first
Pass, sales must be growing
Wait until sales turn up
Buy it, but at half size

wrong.Wait until sales turn up: That's not a rule. The chart sets the entry.
wrong.Buy it, but at half size: No rule halves the size for a sales dip. The size comes from the stop.
wrong.Pass, sales must be growing: Growth is preferred, not required. A real catalyst counts.

questions.why: Buy it. The chart comes first. We like growing sales and earnings, but that's a preference, not a must. A real catalyst counts too, and a big new contract is a real change in the business. The chart shows what buyers are doing right now, and they just doubled this stock in seven weeks. Skip a clean chart over one soft quarter and you're trading a rule we don't have.

questions.simple: Buy it. Growth is preferred, not required, and the chart shows what buyers are doing now.

A big new contract is a real change in the business, so the setup keeps its place. Skipping a clean chart over one soft quarter would be a rule we do not have.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (D40, preferred not required)

questions.q: You buy at 100.00. The flag's low is 88.00. If you put your stop there, how far under your fill is it?
questions.why: 12.0%. Fill minus stop, 100.00 minus 88.00, divided by the fill. I like stops of 1-3%, I'll take up to 5%, and past 5% I wait for a tighter trigger. A 12% stop means a tiny size or no trade at all. That's why the stop goes a few cents under the low of the day, not at the flag low. The flag low is where the idea dies, not where you get out.
questions.lesson_line: A flag-low stop sits way off the buy. The low of the day is much closer.
questions.simple: 12.0% under the fill, way past the 5% we'll take. So the stop goes under the low of the day.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (A13)

wrong.13.6%: That divides by the stop. Divide by the fill.
wrong.88.0%: That's the stop as a share of the fill, not the gap.
wrong.120.0%: A decimal slip, one place too far.

questions.q: Bulkowski's own stop for a high tight flag is the bottom of the flag.
questions.why: True. Bulkowski says to use the bottom of the congestion area formed in the flag phase as the stop price. Ours is different: the primary stop is a few cents under the day's low. The flag low is an acceptable alternative but often sits far wider.
questions.lesson_line: Bulkowski stops at the flag bottom. Ours is a few cents under the day's low.
questions.simple: True, because Bulkowski puts the stop at the bottom of the flag, but our stop is much closer, under the day's low.

deeper.trap: Copying the textbook stop. Bulkowski's stop is the bottom of the flag, which can sit far more than 3% under the buy. Our rulebook says the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy. A flag-low stop would force a much smaller size or no trade, so the day's low stays our primary stop.

reasons: +3 the key rests on one cited fact (Bulkowski's stop locations page)

questions.q: What's 1R on this trade, in dollars a share?
questions.why: $3.78. One R is what you risk on each share: fill minus stop, 94.93 minus 91.15. We count everything in R because it puts every trade on one scale. A 3R winner made three times what you risked, whatever the stock costs. Breakeven, the report rule and the time stop all run in R, so you want this number the moment you're filled.
questions.lesson_line: 1R is what you risk on each share: fill minus stop.
questions.simple: $3.78. One R is the fill minus the stop, and it puts every trade on one scale.

reasons: rests on a published definition (Van Tharp R-multiple)

wrong.$0.04: That divides the gap by the fill, a fraction, not dollars.
wrong.$98.71: That adds one R to the fill. One R is the gap itself.

questions.story: You bought the breakout at 94.93 with the stop at 91.15.

deeper.counter: Van Tharp: all profits and losses can be expressed as a multiple of the initial risk, R.

questions.q: On our card, does this flag pass the fast-averages check?
questions.story: A stock nearly doubled in seven weeks, then paused 12 sessions a little under its high. One close in that pause sat under the 21-day EMA. Today it trades through the high.
choices: No, the card allows zero such closes
Yes, one dip is fine above the 50-day
Yes, if both averages are rising now
No, it paused too long to count
questions.answer: No, the card allows zero such closes
questions.why: No. On our card, no close in the flag may sit below the 21-day EMA. At the trigger, price must also be above a rising 10-day and a rising 21-day EMA. Rising means higher than 5 sessions ago. Both halves count.
questions.lesson_line: On our card, the flag rides rising fast averages and never closes under the 21-day EMA.

wrong.Yes, one dip is fine above the 50-day: The 50-day is a separate check on our card. The flag line is no close under the 21-day EMA.
wrong.Yes, if both averages are rising now: Rising averages are only half the line. Our card also wants no flag close under the 21-day EMA.
wrong.No, it paused too long to count: Our card allows a pause of 5 to 30 sessions. A 12-session pause sits inside that.

questions.simple: No, because our card allows no close in the flag below the 21-day EMA.

questions.q: Can you move the stop to breakeven now?
questions.story: You bought the breakout at 175.81 with the stop at 168.86. It's now up 2R, and you haven't sold a share.
choices: Yes, 2R is inside the window
No, only after the first sell
No, it has to wait for 5R
Yes, but only on heavy volume
questions.why: Yes. The stop can go to breakeven anywhere from 2R to 5R, or at the first sell. You're at 2R, so you're in the window. It's your call, not a must. Move it and a trade that was up 2R can't turn into a loss, unless a gap jumps the stop. The cost is you might get shaken out of a good one on a normal pullback. Either way, the stop only moves up.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven is allowed anywhere from 2R to 5R. It doesn't wait for a sale.

wrong.Yes, but only on heavy volume: Breakeven goes by how far you're up in R, not volume.
wrong.No, only after the first sell: The window opens at 2R. It doesn't wait for a sale.
wrong.No, it has to wait for 5R: 5R is the late end of the window, not the start.

questions.simple: Yes. Breakeven is allowed from 2R to 5R, so a winner doesn't turn into a loss.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, breakeven at 2R to 5R ideally) and the card's default (at the first trim)
+1 the key says the move is allowed at 2R, not that 2R is the default; the MRVL conflict asks whether 2R should become the default

questions.q: The flag checks out. What do you do?
questions.story: The day before the breakout. The flag's high is 94.92, and today is a quiet inside day a few points under it. Next morning, in regular hours, it trades through 94.92.
choices: Buy at market, stop under the day's low
Wait for a close over 94.92
Bid under 94.92 for a dip
Buy now, set the stop after the close
questions.answer: Buy at market, stop under the day's low
questions.why: Buy at market as it goes through 94.92. Put the real stop in at once, a few cents under the low of the day. That's the spot you trade against. Today's inside day helps. A quiet day inside yesterday's range, near the high, is a good look before a buy day. We buy as price trades through, during the day, never at the close. Wait for the close and you pay more, with the stop farther away, so fewer shares. A bid under the high may never fill. Set the alert at 94.92 the night before.
questions.lesson_line: Buy as it trades through the top. The stop goes in with the buy.
questions.simple: Buy at market as it trades through the flag's high, and put the stop in at once, under the day's low.

wrong.Wait for a close over 94.92: We buy through the trigger during the day, never at the close. By then you've paid up.
wrong.Bid under 94.92 for a dip: A bid under the trigger may never fill. It's already going.
wrong.Buy now, set the stop after the close: The stop goes in with the buy. Until it's in, the position has no exit.

deeper.counter: Bulkowski's close above the top confirms the pattern is valid. Our buy doesn't wait for it.

questions.q: What kind of run came right before this rest?
questions.story: The day before the breakout. A leader has paused near its high. Look at what it did right before the pause.
choices: A fast climb of almost a double
A slow grind of about a fifth
A crash, then a bounce back up
Months of tight sideways trading
questions.answer: A fast climb of almost a double
questions.why: A fast climb of almost a double. SOFI ran 91% in 28 sessions. That's the pole. A run like that shows heavy buying, and a rest that holds near the high shows the holders aren't selling. No fast run, nothing to rest from. A slow grind into a pause is just a pullback, and a bounce off a crash is a repair.

wrong.A slow grind of about a fifth: A slow grind has nothing to rest from. This run was fast, nearly a double in weeks.
wrong.A crash, then a bounce back up: That's a V off a crash, a repair job, not a launch.
wrong.Months of tight sideways trading: A long quiet box is a base. The pole is the fast climb before the rest.

questions.simple: A fast climb of almost a double. A rest after a hurried run shows the holders aren't selling.
questions.lesson_line: No fast run, nothing to rest from. The pole comes first.

reasons: the figures are read off our own daily bars; the exact pole size differs by source and is not the key

deeper.counter: IBD describes a gain of 100% to 120% in four to eight weeks. Bulkowski wants at least 90%, shooting for a double, in 2 months or less.

questions.q: One heavy-volume down day shows up in the rest. That kills the high tight flag.
questions.why: False. One heavy down day in the rest doesn't kill it. It's a distribution day, a day some holders sold in size. Be mindful of it. It's a warning, and it can lower the grade, which means a smaller size. But one day doesn't show the pause has failed. Watch the next few days. If the closes hold tight near the high, the holders are still there.
questions.simple: False. One heavy down day is a warning and can lower the grade, but it doesn't kill the setup.
questions.lesson_line: A heavy down day in the rest is a warning and a lower grade, never a ban.

reasons: rests on his ruling that a heavy-volume down day never voids a setup (2026-11-14)

questions.q: How does the grade change the size of each?
questions.story: We grade every setup A+, A, B or B-. The grade is your judgment of how clean it looks, with no checklist. Two high tight flags trigger today. You grade one A+ and the other B-.
choices: Size the A+ up and the B- down
The same size for both of them
Size the B- up for more upside
Take the A+ only, never a B-
questions.answer: Size the A+ up and the B- down
questions.why: Size the A+ up and the B- down. The grade sets the size. A and B go on at normal size, A+ gets sized up, and B- or lower gets sized down. In risk terms, A+ runs 1% to 1.5% of the account and B- runs 0.25% to 0.5%. The cleaner setup has earned more risk. The shakier one gets less, so if it fails it costs little. There's no checklist for the grade. It's your judgment.

wrong.The same size for both of them: The grade exists to change the size. Cleaner setups get more risk.
wrong.Size the B- up for more upside: A weaker grade gets less risk, not more.
wrong.Take the A+ only, never a B-: A B- isn't banned. It's sized down, so a failure costs little.

questions.simple: A+ gets more size and B- gets less, because a cleaner setup has earned more risk.
questions.lesson_line: A cleaner setup earns more size. A shakier one earns less.
